an0375.user: I'm running Google Performance Max for my home-care brand, spent about ₹18L last 30 days. The thing driving me mad is my two dashboards. The ad platform is telling me ROAS is 3.9, looks brilliant. But when I open Shopify and look at last-click it says 1.8. Which one do I actually believe? I genuinely can't tell which number is real and I'm making budget decisions off this.
an0375.assistant:
Neither number is "real" — that's the part nobody tells new founders. The platform's 3.9 is modelled conversions on a 7-day click window, post-iOS, so it generously claims credit for sales it merely touched. Shopify last-click at 1.8 is the opposite bias: it hands all the credit to whoever the customer clicked last, usually a branded search or a retargeting ad, and starves the top-of-funnel work that actually started the journey. The truth sits somewhere between 1.8 and 3.9, and those two dashboards will never agree because they're answering different questions.

So stop refereeing them. The metric you can actually trust is blended CAC: total spend ÷ the real new customers Shopify shows you acquired that month. ₹18L ÷ your genuine new-customer count gives you one honest cost-to-acquire that no attribution model can inflate. Manage the account to that number — if blended CAC is below your contribution per order, keep spending; if not, pull back.

Caveat: blended CAC blurs new vs. returning, so tag new customers in Shopify cleanly or the denominator lies to you too. But it's a far steadier steering wheel than two ROAS dashboards fighting each other.

The leak is behind the door. Your 90-day repeat rate is 10%. That means roughly nine of every ten customers you pay ₹606 to acquire buy once and vanish. You're not building an annuity, you're renting one-time transactions at a profit so thin that one bad CAC month wipes it out. That's why the cash isn't compounding even though the dashboard looks fine.

Don't touch the spend yet. Fix activation and second-order conversion first — onboarding, the first integration milestone, the nudge that gets a developer to actually ship with your API. Scaling acquisition now just pours more water into a bucket with no bottom.

One honest caveat: 10% over 90 days might partly be a window problem if your real usage cycle is longer than a quarter. Check whether "repeat" is even the right horizon for your billing before you conclude the bucket's empty.

an0377.user: Running WhatsApp broadcasts for my skincare line and the top-line numbers actually look strong to me. Around 9.1 lakh impressions, just under 12,000 clicks, CTR sitting at 1.3%. But it converted to only 131 orders at ₹2050 AOV. I keep pushing reach because the clicks come in fine. Where's this falling apart — is it a pricing thing on the landing page?
an0377.assistant:
It's not the landing page, and it's not your CTR. Run the funnel: 11,983 clicks turned into 131 orders, a 1.09% conversion rate. People are clicking in volume and almost none are buying. That's the signature of low-intent traffic — you're broad-matching, casting wide, and pulling in browsers who tapped out of curiosity, not buyers who came to purchase.

The tell is the gap between a perfectly normal 1.3% CTR and that floor-level 1.09% conversion. If pricing or the page were the problem, you'd see decent intent traffic stalling at checkout. Instead the intent never shows up — you're buying clicks, not customers. Reach is exactly the wrong lever here; more of the same broad audience just buys more tyre-kickers.

Tighten intent. Cut the broad-match net, build lists/segments around people who've shown actual buying signals — past purchasers, cart-abandoners, lookalikes of buyers not clickers — add negatives for the junk queries, and stop letting the platform optimise for the cheap click. Fewer, hotter taps will out-convert this volume easily.

Caveat: confirm the page itself isn't quietly broken on mobile before you blame intent entirely — but with conversion this far below CTR, the smart money is on who you're reaching, not what they land on.

The lever: tighten the audience to high-intent, in-market, geo-fenced around your actual locations, and add negatives so the broad junk drops out. Trade some of that 2% CTR for traffic that walks in the door.

The question isn't "how do I lower CAC," it's "why am I selling at 25% margin?"

The lever sits upstream of Meta entirely: fix the economics — negotiate COGS down, raise price, or lift AOV through bundles/higher-value SKUs — until contribution before CAC is comfortably above ₹665. On Meesho's price-sensitive buyers that's hard, which is exactly the point: paid acquisition may not be a viable channel for this product at this margin.

Caveat: if a chunk of these buyers repeat, second-order contribution could change the maths — but on a single 30-day snapshot, the loss per order is real and the margin is the thing to fix.
